opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been interesting because when you put something like this out in the open, people immediately take it in directions you didn't anticipate. Early on, the core priority was pretty simple: can we get a model that doesn't fit on one machine to run across a handful of devices you already own, a couple of MacBooks, a Mac mini, maybe a Linux box with a GPU, and have it just work without a bunch of configuration. That "just works" part was really the north star.

As people started using it, we saw a few distinct camps emerge. There are the hobbyists and tinkerers who want to run the biggest open-weight model they can at home, and for them the priority is really about capacity and ease of setup. Then there's a group that cares a lot about privacy, small companies, research labs, people in regulated settings who don't want data leaving the building. For them, reliability and predictable performance matter much more than squeezing out the last token per second. And then there are people pushing on throughput, trying to serve multiple users or run agentic workloads where you're making tons of calls.

Those groups pull you in different directions. The hobbyist wants heterogeneous device support, everything from phones to old laptops. The throughput crowd wants us to be smart about networking, because once you split a model across machines, the interconnect becomes the bottleneck pretty quickly. So a lot of our focus has shifted toward the systems side: how you partition the model given the actual bandwidth and latency between devices, how you handle a device dropping off, how you schedule work so you're not leaving compute idle.

I think the honest answer is that the priorities are becoming less about "can we run it at all" and more about "can we run it well, under real conditions." That means better observability so people understand where their performance is going, better defaults so people don't have to be distributed systems experts, and being a good citizen in the broader ecosystem, playing nicely with standard APIs so you can drop it in where you'd otherwise call a hosted endpoint.

And longer term, the thing I find most exciting is that the more people use it for different purposes, the more it becomes a testbed for the question of whether a lot of inference can move to the edge, onto hardware people already own, rather than everything being centralized. Letting usage guide us there, rather than guessing, has been the right call.

r001.rationale: The response describes priorities shifting as people use Exo for varied, real-world workloads, then identifies ecosystem compatibility and standard APIs as a priority so Exo can replace hosted endpoints.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we started Exo, the thesis was really simple: people have a lot of compute sitting around in their homes and offices that's basically idle. Your MacBook, your old gaming PC, maybe a Mac Mini you bought for a side project. Individually, none of those can run a frontier-class model. Together, they actually can. So the early priorities were almost entirely about the plumbing. Can we discover devices on a network automatically? Can we partition a model across heterogeneous hardware, where one node is an M-series Mac and another is an NVIDIA card with completely different memory and bandwidth characteristics? Can we do that without the user having to think about it?

What's changed is that once that plumbing worked, people started using it in ways we didn't fully anticipate, and that's forcing us to rethink what "done" means for each piece.

The first group is hobbyists and researchers who just want to run the biggest open model they can, locally, for privacy or curiosity. For them, the priority is breadth of model support and making setup trivially easy. If a new model drops on Hugging Face on Tuesday, they want it running on their cluster on Wednesday. So a lot of effort goes into keeping up with architectures and quantization formats, and into making the failure modes legible when something doesn't fit in memory.

The second group surprised us more. It's small teams and startups that look at Exo as a way to avoid paying for cloud inference. They don't care about the elegance of peer-to-peer discovery. They care about throughput, reliability, and whether a node dropping off the network takes down their service. That pushes us toward things that are frankly more boring but more important: fault tolerance, request scheduling, observability, an API that behaves exactly like the OpenAI one so they can swap it in without rewriting code. That's a very different engineering culture than "make it work on three laptops at a hackathon."

And then there's a third thing emerging, which is people using Exo not just for inference but as a substrate for experimentation. Distributed fine-tuning, speculative decoding across devices, trying out pipeline versus tensor parallel strategies on hardware that nobody at a big lab would ever bother to benchmark. That group wants the internals exposed and hackable rather than hidden.

So the honest answer is that the priorities are pulling in a few directions at once, and the way we're trying to resolve that is by being disciplined about the core. The core should stay small: device discovery, topology-aware partitioning, and a clean inference engine abstraction. Everything that's specific to a use case lives on top of that, ideally as something the community can own. If we try to be the best at all three of those stories simultaneously, we'll be mediocre at all of them. If we nail the layer that makes a pile of mismatched consumer hardware look like one coherent machine, I think the rest follows.

The other thing I'd say is that the hardware is moving toward us. Unified memory on Apple silicon, the consumer boxes with large memory pools, even phones getting serious NPUs. Every one of those changes makes the "connect what you already have" story more compelling, and it means our roadmap is partly dictated by what shows up in people's homes over the next couple of years rather than by what we decide in a planning doc.

r001.rationale: The response says that as Exo moved beyond its initial plumbing and small teams began using it to replace cloud inference, priorities shifted toward production needs, including an OpenAI-compatible API that teams can swap in without rewriting code.

astra-6.text:
I think the priorities will become much clearer as we see what people actually want to do with it. Someone experimenting with models on machines they already own may care most about how easy it is to get started. Someone building an application may care much more about reliability and performance. Those uses push you toward different things.

So I’d want us to stay close to users and understand where they’re getting stuck. What takes too much setup? What can’t they run yet? Where is it too slow? That feedback should help us decide what to build next, while keeping the core experience simple enough that people can keep experimenting.

r001.rationale: The response mentions ease of getting started and keeping the experience simple, but it does not present Exo’s maturation in production as the reason to make integration easier.

sol-6.1.text: I think a lot of that will come from seeing what people actually do with it. Different use cases will expose different bottlenecks: some people will care most about performance, while others will care about how easy it is to get started or whether their setup works reliably. So the priorities will evolve with that feedback. The challenge is figuring out which improvements help broadly and which are specific to one use case, and keeping the core simple enough that people can build in directions we haven’t anticipated.

r001.rationale: The response mentions ease of getting started and adapting to user feedback, but does not say Exo is maturing in production or connect that maturation to making integration easier for others.
